title: The Council at Medicine Lodge Creek
subtitle: The Indian Peace Commission and the Kiowa, Comanche, Plains Apache, Cheyenne and Arapaho, southern Kansas, 1867
span: October 1867 (Sand Creek 1864 to Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock 1903)
intro: In October 1867 some five thousand Gáuigú (Kiowa), Nʉmʉnʉʉ (Comanche), Na'isha (Plains Apache, the record's 'Kiowa-Apache'), Hinono'ei (Arapaho) and Tsitsistas (Cheyenne) people camped along Medicine Lodge Creek in southern Kansas, where it meets Elm Creek, to meet the Indian Peace Commission. The commission had been created by Congress that July to end three years of war on the Plains and to clear the way for railroads and settlement. It came south from Fort Larned with a train of 165 wagons, a cavalry escort, and a press corps.

The war had a beginning everyone at the council knew. In November 1864 Colorado volunteers under John Chivington attacked Black Kettle's Cheyenne and Arapaho camp at Sand Creek after its people had been told they were under protection. The commission's own report of January 1868 called it a massacre. At Medicine Lodge a Cheyenne man turned the commissioners' pipe bowl down because his father had died there, and Little Raven named it in his speech.

The council produced three treaties. On 21 October the Kiowa and Comanche signed one, and the Plains Apache a second that joined them to it. On 28 October, after the main Cheyenne bands finally came in from the Cimarron, the Cheyenne and Arapaho signed a joint treaty. The nations gave up claims to the country north of the new reservations in the Indian Territory and were promised houses, schools, farming tools, clothing and money for thirty years. They kept a right to hunt south of the Arkansas only while the buffalo lasted. Article 12 of each treaty barred any future cession without the consent of three-fourths of the adult men.

Almost none of the record is a diary. The state's side is the commission's journal, kept by its secretary and a shorthand reporter, the treaty texts, and the report to the President. The press is unusually rich: a dozen correspondents, among them a 26-year-old Henry M. Stanley, took the speeches down at tables under the brush arbour. Every Indigenous speech survives only as an interpreter's English taken down by the other side. The interpreters included Philip McCusker for the Comanche, John S. Smith and George Bent for the Cheyenne, and others. Popular modern versions of Satanta's and Ten Bears's speeches are often embellished. This chapter uses only wording from 1867 reports and labels it as interpreted.

The Indigenous record also survives in other forms. The Kiowa kept pictographic calendars, and Set-t'an's names this season 'Timber-hill winter' for the wooded hill at the treaty ground, while another Kiowa calendar ignores the treaty altogether. George Bent, the Cheyenne-born interpreter, wrote his memories down forty years later. Two late memoirs, by Bent and by the commissioner's son Alfred Taylor, add camp detail the official papers leave out. They are labelled as late.

The epilogue is a court case. In 1903, in Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock, the Supreme Court considered the Kiowa claim that the allotment of their reservation without three-fourths consent broke Article 12. It held that Congress could set treaty provisions aside. The promise made aloud to the Cheyenne about hunting north of the Arkansas, which a reporter asked to have written in, belongs to the same story of spoken and written treaties.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian. The council's key days fell as follows: the grand council opened on Saturday 19 October, the Kiowa and Comanche treaty was signed on Monday 21 October, the Cheyenne came in on Sunday 27 October, and their treaty was signed on Monday 28 October 1867. The Kiowa calendars count two seasons a year, each named for an event; 'Winter 1867–68' and 'Summer 1868' are given here as ranges with a nominal sortable date. A. A. Taylor's 1924 memoir names weekdays for the Cheyenne arrival that do not fit the calendar, and his dates are marked approximate.

eyes.name: Nathaniel Green Taylor
eyes.role: US Commissioner of Indian Affairs, aged 48; former Methodist preacher and Tennessee congressman; president of the Indian Peace Commission
eyes.where: Fort Larned, then the commission camp on Medicine Lodge Creek; Washington for the report
eyes.vantage_label: president of the commission that ran the council
eyes.form: speeches as reported in the press; treaty signatures; official report
eyes.authenticity: His council words survive as correspondents and the commission's secretary took them down; the commission's report of 7 Jan 1868 was printed by Congress and is reproduced on Wikisource. The report is signed by all eight commissioners, including Sherman, who was not at Medicine Lodge.
eyes.bio: Taylor was the civilian head of the Indian Office and the commission's president, a reformer who believed peace and 'civilization' could replace war on the Plains. His report, unusually for a government document, laid much of the blame for the wars of 1864–67 on the United States, naming Sand Creek a massacre. His son Alfred came with him to the council as an assistant secretary.

sources.title: Report to the President by the Indian Peace Commission, January 7, 1868 (Wikisource)
New York Daily Tribune, 23 Oct 1867 (transcription)

eyes.name: John Brooks Henderson
eyes.role: US Senator from Missouri, aged 41; chairman of the Senate Committee on Indian Affairs and author of the bill that created the commission
eyes.where: Washington, then the council ground on Medicine Lodge Creek
eyes.vantage_label: chief negotiator who set out the terms
eyes.form: speeches as reported in the press and the commission journal
eyes.authenticity: No diary. His speeches survive in the commission's journal (published in 1975 as Proceedings of the Great Peace Commission, ed. Vine Deloria Jr. and Raymond DeMallie) and in correspondents' dispatches. His spoken promise about hunting north of the Arkansas is known from the press, not the treaty text.
eyes.bio: Henderson, best remembered for co-writing the Thirteenth Amendment, carried the peace bill through the Senate in July 1867 and did most of the commission's talking at Medicine Lodge. He laid out reservations, houses, schools, farms and annuities, and on the last day gave the Cheyenne a spoken assurance about hunting that the written treaty did not contain.

sources.title: NPS Washita Battlefield, October 1867
Treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, 1867 (Kappler text)

eyes.name: Ashton S. H. White
eyes.role: Secretary of the Indian Peace Commission, keeper of its official journal, working with the shorthand reporter ('phonographer') George B. Willis
eyes.where: The council arbour on Medicine Lodge Creek
eyes.vantage_label: official recorder at the council table
eyes.authenticity: The manuscript journal of the commission's proceedings is held in the National Archives (Records of the Bureau of Indian Affairs) and was published in 1975 as Proceedings of the Great Peace Commission of 1867–1868. Every Indigenous speech in it is the interpreter's English as taken down at the table. White signs the Cheyenne and Arapaho treaty as secretary; Willis signs as phonographer.
eyes.bio: White's journal is the nearest thing to a minute of the council: it records who spoke, in what order, and through which interpreter. Its English is a double filter, the interpreter's rendering and then the secretary's or stenographer's pen, which is why the press versions of the same speeches often differ in wording.

sources.title: Treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, 1867 — witness list (Kappler text)

eyes.name: Henry Morton Stanley
eyes.role: Newspaper correspondent, aged 26; Welsh-born, recently a Civil War soldier and sailor; later the journalist who found Livingstone
eyes.side: Press (St. Louis and New York papers)
eyes.where: With the commission's column and at the council ground
eyes.authenticity: Sources disagree on which papers he wrote for: American Heritage (1978) names the Weekly Missouri Democrat; A. A. Taylor (1924) and a 1927 Kansas article name the New York Tribune; a 1927 House report says the Cincinnati Commercial. He sent dispatches to more than one paper. The unsigned New York Daily Tribune dispatch of 15 Oct used here is attributed to him only on Taylor's word. His dispatches were reprinted in his 'My Early Travels and Adventures in America and Asia' (1895) and in the Kansas Historical Quarterly (Autumn 1967). He signs the Cheyenne and Arapaho treaty as 'Henry Stanley, correspondent'.
eyes.bio: Stanley was an unknown freelance when he rode south with the commission; his Medicine Lodge reports helped make his name. He wrote quickly and vividly, recording speeches as interpreted at the arbour, and his texts are among the main sources for what Satanta and Ten Bears said.

sources.title: My early travels and adventures in America and Asia, v.1 (1895), Smithsonian Libraries
Kansas Historical Quarterly, Autumn 1967 (Stanley's Medicine Lodge reports)
T. H. Watkins, 'Chief Satanta, I Presume?', American Heritage 29:6 (1978)

eyes.name: William Fayel
eyes.role: Correspondent of the Missouri Republican (St. Louis)
eyes.where: At the Cheyenne council, Medicine Lodge Creek
eyes.authenticity: Known here through Douglas C. Jones's eyewitness compilation The Treaty of Medicine Lodge (1966), as summarised by the National Park Service; his original dispatches were not consulted.
eyes.bio: Fayel is the reporter who, by the press record, noticed that Henderson's spoken promise about hunting north of the Arkansas was not in the paper the Cheyenne were about to sign, and asked for the wording to be changed. His question is one of the clearest moments where the spoken and written treaties part company.

sources.title: NPS Washita Battlefield, October 1867

eyes.name: Alfred Alexander Taylor
eyes.role: Aged 19, son of Commissioner N. G. Taylor, appointed an assistant secretary to the commission; later Governor of Tennessee (1921–23)
eyes.where: With the column from Fort Harker and in the camp at Medicine Lodge Creek
eyes.vantage_label: young staff member, remembering 57 years on
eyes.authenticity: Written in 1924 for the Chronicles of Oklahoma. It is vivid but late: some details do not fit the contemporary record (his weekdays for the Cheyenne arrival do not match the calendar, and he places Stanley on the New York Tribune). He signs the Cheyenne and Arapaho treaty as a witness, 'A. A. Taylor'.
eyes.bio: Taylor's recollection gives the camp life the official journal leaves out: Harney's display of the column, gift-giving, a dog feast, a false alarm, and the drama of the Cheyenne arrival. He was the last surviving member of the party when he wrote it.

sources.title: A. A. Taylor, 'Medicine Lodge Peace Council', Chronicles of Oklahoma 2:2 (1924)

eyes.name: George Bent
eyes.role: Aged 24; son of the trader William Bent and Owl Woman (Tsitsistas); survivor of Sand Creek; interpreter for the Cheyenne and Arapaho agent Edward Wynkoop
eyes.side: Tsitsistas (Cheyenne) kin; interpreter for the United States
eyes.where: Southern Plains camps, Fort Larned, Medicine Lodge Creek
eyes.vantage_label: Cheyenne-born interpreter between the two sides
eyes.authenticity: His account appeared as 'Forty Years with the Cheyennes' in the magazine The Frontier (the reprint cites February 1909) and was reprinted in the Barber County Index, 29 Sept 1927 (citing The Frontier, Feb. 1909). His much fuller letters to George Hyde were published in 1968 as Life of George Bent. He signs the Cheyenne and Arapaho treaty as interpreter.
eyes.bio: Bent stood on both sides of the council: raised among his mother's people, he had been in Black Kettle's camp at Sand Creek, then rode with the Dog Soldiers, and by 1867 was interpreting for the government. His account explains how the camps were placed and which Cheyenne leaders carried the peace.

sources.title: George Bent, 'The Medicine Lodge Peace Council' (reprint, Barber County Index 1927)

eyes.name: Set'tainte (Satanta, 'White Bear')
eyes.role: Kiowa war leader and orator, about 47; one of the leading men after the death of Dohásän in 1866
eyes.where: Kiowa camp below the council ground, Medicine Lodge Creek
eyes.authenticity: His words survive only in interpreters' English as taken down by reporters and the commission's secretary. Embellished modern versions circulate widely; one popular line, that settling down makes his people 'grow pale and die', could not be placed in an 1867 text for this chapter. Only phrasing found in 1867 reports is used here.
eyes.bio: Satanta was the most quoted Indigenous speaker at Medicine Lodge, defiant about land and buffalo and scornful of houses and schools, yet he signed on 21 October. Four years later he was tried in Texas for the Warren wagon-train raid; he died in the Huntsville prison in 1878 and was reburied at Fort Sill in 1963.

sources.title: New York Daily Tribune, 23 Oct 1867 (transcription)
Texas State Library and Archives, Satanta

eyes.name: Parra-wa-samen (Ten Bears)
eyes.role: Yamparika Comanche leader in his seventies; had visited Washington in 1863
eyes.authenticity: Survives in interpreted English in the commission journal and press reports; the Comanche interpreter at the council was Philip McCusker, who also witnessed the treaty. The text is often reprinted with small variations ('born on the prairie' / 'born upon the prairie'); a 1927 Kansas newspaper reprint is the version consulted here. Mooney's treaty list renders his name Päriăséaman, 'Ten-elks'.
eyes.bio: Ten Bears was an elder statesman who had seen Washington and returned unconvinced. His speech at Medicine Lodge, protesting houses and fixed reservations and recalling a life on the open prairie, became the most reprinted Indigenous oration of the council. He went to Washington again in 1872 and died that year near Fort Sill.

sources.title: 'Ten Bears, Comanche Chief, Made an Eloquent Address' (Barber County Index, 1927, transcription)
Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (1898)

eyes.name: Moke-tav-a-to (Black Kettle)
eyes.role: Tsitsistas council chief in his sixties; leader of the camp attacked at Sand Creek in November 1864
eyes.where: Cheyenne camp, then the council ground
eyes.authenticity: He said little at the arbour; his part survives mostly as others describe it (correspondents, A. A. Taylor, the commission journal) and in his treaty mark as Moke-tav-a-to.
eyes.bio: Black Kettle had flown a US flag over his lodge at Sand Creek and still argued for peace afterwards, which cost him standing among the soldier societies. At Medicine Lodge he was the commission's link to the main Cheyenne camp on the Cimarron, riding back and forth until the bands came in. A year after signing he was killed when the 7th Cavalry attacked his village on the Washita.

sources.title: NPS Washita Battlefield, October 1867

eyes.name: Hosa (Little Raven)
eyes.role: Principal chief of the Southern Hinono'ei (Arapaho), in his fifties; signer of the Fort Wise (1861) and Little Arkansas (1865) treaties
eyes.where: Arapaho camp just above the council ground
eyes.authenticity: His speech survives in interpreted English in the commission journal and press; A. A. Taylor's 1924 memoir summarises it. The record calls his people Arapahoe.
eyes.bio: Little Raven was known as a skilled diplomat and a peace leader; his band had been camped away from the lodges struck at Sand Creek. At Medicine Lodge he pressed for damages and unpaid annuities and named the massacre. He later spoke at Cooper Union in New York (1871) and kept his people out of the Red River War.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture: Little Raven
Denver Public Library: Chief Little Raven

eyes.name: Is-se-von-ne-ve (Buffalo Chief)
eyes.role: Tsitsistas (Cheyenne) chief who spoke for the Cheyenne at the final council
eyes.vantage_label: Cheyenne spokesman on the last day
eyes.authenticity: His reply to Henderson survives in interpreted English (the Cheyenne interpreter of record was John S. Smith, with George Bent) as reported by correspondents and summarised by Jones (1966) and the National Park Service. He signs the treaty as Is-se-von-ne-ve.
eyes.bio: Buffalo Chief answered Henderson's demand that the Cheyenne give up the country between the Arkansas and the Platte by claiming it as theirs, and set out the Cheyenne understanding that they would keep hunting there. His words mark the clearest gap between what the Cheyenne said they were agreeing to and what the paper said.

sources.title: NPS Washita Battlefield, October 1867
Treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, 1867 (Kappler text)

eyes.name: Set-t'an (Little Bear)
eyes.role: Kiowa calendar keeper whose pictographic year-count runs from the 1830s to the 1890s
eyes.authenticity: Mooney collected the Set-t'an and Anko calendars on the Kiowa reservation in the 1890s and published them, with Kiowa names for each season and his own commentary, in the Bureau of American Ethnology's 17th Annual Report (1898). The pictures are Kiowa; the readings were given to Mooney by Kiowa informants.
eyes.bio: The Kiowa named each summer and winter by its most memorable event and drew it in a single picture. Set-t'an's calendar remembers the Medicine Lodge winter by a handshake under a wooded hill; the Anko calendar, kept by another Kiowa, ignores the treaty altogether and remembers a small raid instead. Together they show how the council sat within a Kiowa year.

sources.title: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (1898), Project Gutenberg
Calendar history of the Kiowa Indians, Smithsonian Research Online

eyes.name: Edward Douglass White
eyes.role: Associate Justice of the US Supreme Court, aged 57, writing for the Court
eyes.authenticity: Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock, 187 U.S. 553, decided 5 January 1903; the opinion is a public US government record.
eyes.bio: The case was brought by the Kiowa leader Lone Wolf (the younger) and others, who argued that the 1900 allotment of the Kiowa, Comanche and Apache reservation broke Article 12 of the Medicine Lodge treaty, which required the consent of three-fourths of the adult men to any cession. White's opinion held that Congress had plenary power over tribal relations and could abrogate treaty provisions, a ruling that shaped federal Indian law for decades.

sources.title: Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture: Medicine Lodge Treaty

entries.headline: Summer 1867: horses stolen, a warrior society initiated
entries.digest: Before the council, the Kiowa remembered the summer of 1867 for horses stolen by the Navajo and the initiation of new members into the Kâitséñko, the Kiowa's highest warrior society. Nothing in the picture points to the peace commission then being organised in Washington and St. Louis.
entries.source_note: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (BAE 17th Annual Report, 1898), Project Gutenberg #46479, fig. 141, pp. 319–320

entries.headline: Congress creates a peace commission for the Plains
entries.digest: Henderson's bill to 'establish peace with certain hostile Indian tribes' became law, authorising a commission of four civilians and up to four generals. Its purpose was to remove the causes of war, secure the frontier settlements, and clear the way for the railroads, and to propose reservations where the nations would be taught to farm. The southern and northern Plains councils of that autumn both grew out of this act.
entries.source_note: Act of 20 July 1867 (15 Stat. 17); NPS 'October 1867' page

entries.place: Camp near present Wichita, then Fort Larned
entries.headline: An interpreter is sent to fetch the chiefs
entries.digest: Bent, interpreting for agent Wynkoop, met Colonel Leavenworth, the Kiowa and Comanche agent, at a camp near present Wichita and was ordered to take chiefs to Fort Larned. He objected that he had never been inside a fort and that, after the summer's fighting, it was not safe for him among the soldiers, but he went. The episode shows how much the council depended on a handful of mixed-descent go-betweens.
entries.source_note: Bent, 'Forty Years with the Cheyennes', The Frontier, reprinted Barber County Index 29 Sept 1927

entries.place: Fort Harker to Fort Larned, Kansas
entries.headline: Harney puts the whole column on show
entries.digest: Taylor remembered the column leaving the railhead around the first of October, with General Harney in command of the march. Wary of the nations they were going to meet, Harney had the wagons and troops strung out in a long S so that watchers on the hills would see the full strength of the escort. It was a peace mission arranged to look like an army.

entries.headline: Seventeen guns and a cavalry band at Fort Harker
entries.digest: The commission's party reached Fort Harker at night to a seventeen-gun salute, and the 7th Cavalry band played until midnight. Next morning they set out for Fort Larned, eighty miles on, with an escort. The dispatch reads like a society column for the first days, before the plains change its tone.
entries.source_note: New York Daily Tribune, 23 Oct 1867, 'Near Texas Line, Oct. 15' dispatch from our Special Correspondent (transcription, ksgenweb.org Barber County); attribution to Stanley rests on A. A. Taylor's statement that he wrote for the Tribune

entries.place: Rattlesnake Creek, south of the Arkansas
entries.headline: Buffalo cover the prairie; a reporter shoots one
entries.digest: South of Fort Larned the column rode through buffalo so thick they covered the prairie, and the artist Jack Howland shot one in defiance of orders against firing. That night at Rattlesnake Creek, Satanta, Little Raven and two Apache chiefs rode into camp to meet the commissioners. The train had grown to 175 wagons and ambulances.
entries.source_note: New York Daily Tribune, 23 Oct 1867, 'Near Texas Line, Oct. 15' dispatch from our Special Correspondent (transcription, ksgenweb.org Barber County)

entries.headline: Little Raven rides out to meet the commissioners
entries.digest: Little Raven, head chief of the Arapaho, came to the commission's camp at Rattlesnake Creek with Satanta and two Plains Apache chiefs, a day's ride before the council ground. Arriving early and in the open was itself a statement: his people had already come in and were camped on Medicine Lodge Creek.
entries.source_note: New York Daily Tribune, 23 Oct 1867, 'Near Texas Line, Oct. 15' dispatch from our Special Correspondent (transcription, ksgenweb.org Barber County)

entries.place: Medicine Lodge Creek, eight miles from the villages
entries.headline: Satanta rebukes the soldiers for killing buffalo
entries.digest: As the column reached Medicine Lodge Creek, Satanta complained about the young men who had been shooting buffalo for sport on the march. As interpreted, he asked whether the white man had become a child, and said that when his people killed, they did it in order to live. It was the first of his speeches the reporters took down, and it set the theme of land and buffalo that he returned to at the council.
entries.quote: Has the white man become a child
entries.source_note: New York Daily Tribune, 23 Oct 1867, 'Near Texas Line, Oct. 15' dispatch from our Special Correspondent (transcription, ksgenweb.org Barber County) (Satanta's words as interpreted)

entries.headline: First sight of the villages along the creek
entries.digest: The correspondent described coming in sight of the lodges strung along the creek and the Arapaho village nearest the council ground, and listed the chiefs gathered there. He noted that Black Kettle was present but said he had been deposed for his peaceful views, a garbled report of the split between the peace chiefs and the soldier societies.
entries.source_note: New York Daily Tribune, 23 Oct 1867, 'Near Texas Line, Oct. 15' dispatch from our Special Correspondent (transcription, ksgenweb.org Barber County)

entries.headline: A preliminary council: wait eight days for the Cheyenne
entries.digest: At a preliminary council Taylor told the assembled chiefs, through the interpreter, that the commission had already made peace with the Oglala and Sicangu (Brulé) Lakota on the Platte. The Cheyenne spokesman Big Jake said it would take eight days for all the Cheyenne to come in from the Cimarron, and the commissioners agreed to wait.
entries.quote: Tell them that we have made peace with the Ogallallas and Brules.
entries.source_note: New York Daily Tribune, 23 Oct 1867, 'Near Texas Line, Oct. 15' dispatch from our Special Correspondent (transcription, ksgenweb.org Barber County) (Taylor's words as reported)

entries.headline: Dispatch: the grand council delayed eight days
entries.digest: The dispatch dated this day, 'near Texas line', reported that the grand council would be put off for the Cheyenne, whose leading chiefs were still on the Cimarron. Big Jake offered to send twenty of his men, dressed in cavalry uniforms, to bring the bands in. The report was printed in New York eight days later.
entries.source_note: New York Daily Tribune, 23 Oct 1867, 'Near Texas Line, Oct. 15' dispatch from our Special Correspondent (transcription, ksgenweb.org Barber County)

entries.place: Cheyenne circle near the council ground
entries.headline: White Antelope turns the pipe bowl down
entries.digest: Taylor recalled riding into the Cheyenne circle with Black Kettle as guide, and a Cheyenne man named White Antelope refusing the commissioners' pipe by turning the bowl down. He gave his reasons: a brother killed at Ash Hollow and his father killed at Sand Creek. Harney spent days winning him over with gifts. Sand Creek was in the camp before the commission said a word about it.

entries.headline: A dog feast and a silk hat for Kicking Bird
entries.digest: On the eve of the grand council the young secretary attended a feast in the camps and gave his silk hat to the Kiowa second chief Kicking Bird (T'ené-angópte), who wore it with only a breechcloth. Taylor told it as comedy; it also shows how freely gifts moved in the days before the speeches.
entries.source_note: Taylor 1924, pp. 110–112 (council opened the day after the feast)

entries.headline: The grand council opens under a brush arbour
entries.digest: The formal council opened with the Kiowa, Comanche, Plains Apache and Arapaho, perhaps 5,000 people camped around, and the 7th Cavalry on guard. Taylor, as president, opened the proceedings and the interpreters relayed each sentence in turn. Only two Cheyenne chiefs were present.
entries.source_note: NPS Washita Battlefield, 'October 1867' history page, drawing on Jones, The Treaty of Medicine Lodge (1966), and the Cincinnati Gazette; Indian Peace Commission entry (encyclopedia mirror) gives 19 Oct as opening

entries.headline: The secretary's journal begins the grand council
entries.digest: The commission's journal records the order of the opening day: the commissioners' statements, then each nation's speakers, each through a named interpreter. A shorthand reporter, George B. Willis, took the words down alongside the secretary. This is the text later printed as the Proceedings of the Great Peace Commission.
entries.source_note: Witness list of the Cheyenne and Arapaho treaty (White, secretary; Willis, phonographer); Proceedings of the Great Peace Commission (1975)

entries.headline: Black Kettle sits nearly silent at the opening
entries.digest: Black Kettle and one other Cheyenne chief were the only Tsitsistas at the opening council. He said little, and spent the following days riding between the council and the main Cheyenne camp, trying to bring the other chiefs in. Correspondents read his silence as weakness; it was the position of a man who could not speak for bands that had not yet arrived.
entries.source_note: NPS Washita Battlefield, 'October 1867' history page, drawing on Jones, The Treaty of Medicine Lodge (1966), and the Cincinnati Gazette

entries.headline: Henderson lays out houses, schools and reservations
entries.digest: Henderson set out the government's offer to the Kiowa and Comanche: a reservation in the Indian Territory, houses, schools, farming tools and annual goods, in return for giving up the country further north and leaving the railroads alone. He argued, as the commissioners did throughout, that the buffalo would not last and that farming was the future. The speeches that followed answered him point by point.
entries.source_note: Day per brief and secondary accounts (Jones 1966); content per treaty text and Stanley's reports as summarised in American Heritage (1978)

entries.headline: Satanta: the land south of the Arkansas is ours
entries.digest: In the speech the reporters most wanted, Satanta claimed the land south of the Arkansas for the Kiowa and Comanche and said he would not part with it or the buffalo. As interpreted, he scorned the houses the commissioners offered and said he wanted the children raised as he had been. On the second day of speaking he said the Kiowa had nothing more to add. These are interpreted words, taken down by Stanley and others.
entries.quote: I love the land and the buffalo
entries.source_note: Stanley's dispatch as quoted in American Heritage 29:6 (1978); the date of 20 Oct follows secondary accounts

entries.headline: Ten Bears: born where the wind blew free
entries.digest: The old Yamparika leader began by saying his heart was full of joy at the commissioners' coming, then turned to grievance: soldiers had started the fighting, and he did not want the houses or the fixed reservation being offered. As interpreted, he recalled being born on the open prairie and wanting to die there, and said he had seen Washington and knew the white man's ways. The speech circulates in several slightly different English versions; all are interpreters' renderings.
entries.quote: I was born on the prairie where the wind blew free
entries.source_note: Ten Bears speech as reprinted in the Barber County Index, 29 Sept 1927 (transcription); interpreter Philip McCusker per treaty witness list and Taylor 1924

entries.headline: A reporter's table under the arbour
entries.digest: Tables had been set up for the correspondents at the council, and Stanley wrote down the speeches as they came through the interpreters. He described Satanta's manner as much as his matter, and came away convinced that the Kiowa saw the commissioners as people who had broken promises before.
entries.source_note: American Heritage 29:6 (1978), summarising Stanley's dispatches

entries.headline: Little Raven asks for damages and names Sand Creek
entries.digest: Little Raven spoke for the Arapaho about damages owed to his people, annuities promised and never paid, and the massacre at Sand Creek. Taylor, writing long after, singled out this speech as the finest he heard at the council. Like the others, it reaches us only as an interpreter's English.
entries.source_note: Taylor 1924, pp. 113–114; exact day not established

entries.headline: The Kiowa, Comanche and Plains Apache treaties are signed
entries.digest: The commissioners signed the treaty with the Kiowa and Comanche and, the same day, a supplementary treaty joining the Plains Apache to them. The reservation lay between the 98th meridian, the Red River and its North Fork, and the Washita, with clothing, money and schools promised for thirty and twenty years. The witnesses were Superintendent Thomas Murphy, agent J. H. Leavenworth and the interpreter Philip McCusker.
entries.source_note: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (BAE 17th Annual Report, 1898), Project Gutenberg #46479, pp. 181–186; Kansas Historical Society Kansapedia

entries.headline: Satanta signs after all
entries.digest: Despite his speech of the day before, Satanta put his mark to the treaty, listed by Mooney as Set-t'aiñte, alongside Satank, Kicking Bird, Stumbling Bear and six other Kiowa. Lone Wolf (Gui-pä'go), by the Kansas Historical Society's account, was the one leading Kiowa who did not sign. A last-minute concession allowed hunting on the old ranges south of the Arkansas.
entries.source_note: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (BAE 17th Annual Report, 1898), Project Gutenberg #46479; Kansapedia 'Kiowa - Medicine Lodge Treaty'

entries.headline: Ten Bears signs as Päriăséaman
entries.digest: Ten Bears signed for the Comanche, one of ten Comanche names on the paper. Mooney, listing the signers thirty years later, rendered his name as 'Ten-elks' and noted that of the Comanche signers only one, Howía, was still alive in 1896.
entries.source_note: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (BAE 17th Annual Report, 1898), Project Gutenberg #46479

entries.headline: Black Kettle brings the Cheyenne in
entries.digest: After days away, Black Kettle came back leading the main body of Cheyenne, who arrived in five mounted columns, firing into the air and charging toward the creek before pulling up. Correspondents counted about five hundred men. It was the end of nearly two weeks in which the main Cheyenne camp had stayed some forty miles off, sending small parties to test the commission.
entries.source_note: NPS Washita Battlefield, 'October 1867' history page, drawing on Jones, The Treaty of Medicine Lodge (1966), and the Cincinnati Gazette (correspondent's description of five columns of a hundred men)

entries.headline: A false alarm, then the Cheyenne charge
entries.digest: Taylor remembered Black Kettle promising the Cheyenne for one day and their arriving a day early, and an evening false alarm in which the Comanche interpreter McCusker led the white party to arms. When the Cheyenne finally came in, he wrote, they had certainly fooled the camp. His weekdays (a Tuesday announcement, a Wednesday arrival) do not fit the calendar, since 27 October 1867 was a Sunday: memory compressed the week.

entries.headline: Henderson tells the Cheyenne to give up the north
entries.digest: Henderson told the Cheyenne they must give up the country between the Arkansas and the South Platte and live on a reservation south of Kansas. When the chiefs objected, he promised them privately that they could still hunt north of the Arkansas as long as they lived south of it. That promise was not written into the treaty.
entries.source_note: NPS Washita Battlefield, 'October 1867' history page, drawing on Jones, The Treaty of Medicine Lodge (1966), and the Cincinnati Gazette

entries.headline: Buffalo Chief: the country to the Platte is ours
entries.digest: Answering Henderson, Buffalo Chief said, as interpreted, that the country between the Arkansas and the South Platte belonged to the Cheyenne. He set out the Cheyenne view that they would keep hunting there and wanted the soldiers and roads kept off it. It was the plainest statement at the council that the two sides meant different things by the same paper.
entries.quote: that country between the Arkansas and the South Platte is ours
entries.source_note: NPS Washita Battlefield, 'October 1867' history page, drawing on Jones, The Treaty of Medicine Lodge (1966), and the Cincinnati Gazette (Buffalo Chief's words as interpreted)

entries.headline: A reporter asks to have the promise written in
entries.digest: Fayel, noticing that the spoken assurance about hunting north of the Arkansas was not in the treaty, asked Henderson to change the wording. Henderson refused, telling him it was no time for bickering. The treaty was signed as written.
entries.source_note: NPS Washita Battlefield, 'October 1867' history page, drawing on Jones, The Treaty of Medicine Lodge (1966), and the Cincinnati Gazette, citing Jones (1966)

entries.headline: Buffalo Chief signs as Is-se-von-ne-ve
entries.digest: Despite his objections, Buffalo Chief put his mark on the treaty among fourteen Cheyenne signers, with Black Kettle, Bull Bear, Little Robe, Tall Bull and others. Article 11 reserved hunting only on lands south of the Arkansas, and only while buffalo remained in numbers to justify the chase.
entries.source_note: Treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, 1867, 15 Stat. 593 (Oklahoma State University Tribal Treaties Database, Kappler text)

entries.headline: Black Kettle signs; Little Robe calls it enough
entries.digest: Black Kettle signed as Moke-tav-a-to. Some chiefs held back until Little Robe declared there were enough signatures and others were talked round. Then came the presents, including cheap cast-iron pistols, one of which burst when a Cheyenne man tried it.
entries.source_note: NPS Washita Battlefield, 'October 1867' history page, drawing on Jones, The Treaty of Medicine Lodge (1966), and the Cincinnati Gazette; Treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, 1867, 15 Stat. 593 (Oklahoma State University Tribal Treaties Database, Kappler text)

entries.headline: Little Raven signs for the Arapaho
entries.digest: Little Raven headed the eight Arapaho signers of the joint treaty, which put the Cheyenne and Arapaho on a reservation of about three million acres between the Kansas line, the Arkansas and the Cimarron. It was the same people's third treaty in seven years.
entries.source_note: Treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, 1867, 15 Stat. 593 (Oklahoma State University Tribal Treaties Database, Kappler text)

entries.headline: Interpreting the signing for the Cheyenne
entries.digest: Bent interpreted at the signing, with his brother Charley also present. He recalled that the Dog Soldiers, the strongest of the Cheyenne soldier societies, led the peace party, and that their chiefs Bull Bear, Tall Bull and White Horse signed. His name stands on the treaty as an interpreter beside John S. Smith and C. W. Whitaker.
entries.source_note: Bent, Barber County Index reprint 1927; Treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, 1867, 15 Stat. 593 (Oklahoma State University Tribal Treaties Database, Kappler text)

entries.headline: The secretary and the stenographer witness the treaty
entries.digest: White signed the Cheyenne and Arapaho treaty as the commission's secretary, and George B. Willis as phonographer, together with the interpreters, the clerk J. D. Howland, the surveyor, A. A. Taylor and Henry Stanley. The witness list doubles as a roll of who held the pen and who carried the words.
entries.source_note: Treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, 1867, 15 Stat. 593 (Oklahoma State University Tribal Treaties Database, Kappler text)

entries.headline: The commission's last treaty on the southern Plains
entries.digest: Taylor and the other commissioners signed the joint Cheyenne and Arapaho treaty, closing the council. It was the last treaty the United States made with the southern Plains nations; the commission went on to the north for the Fort Laramie treaty of 1868.
entries.source_note: Treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, 1867, 15 Stat. 593 (Oklahoma State University Tribal Treaties Database, Kappler text); NPS 'October 1867'

entries.headline: Dispatch: peace with all the southern tribes
entries.digest: Stanley's closing report announced that peace had been concluded with all the southern nations. He signed the Cheyenne and Arapaho treaty as a witness, 'Henry Stanley, correspondent'. Within a year he was reporting a new war on the same plains.
entries.quote: Peace has been concluded with all the Southern tribes.
entries.source_note: American Heritage 29:6 (1978) quoting Stanley's dispatch; Treaty with the Cheyenne and Arapaho, 1867, 15 Stat. 593 (Oklahoma State University Tribal Treaties Database, Kappler text)

entries.headline: Timber-hill winter: a soldier grasps an Indian's hand
entries.digest: Set-t'an's calendar names this winter Ä´yä´daldä Sai, 'Timber-hill winter', after the wooded hill at the treaty site, and draws a white man who seems to be a soldier clasping an Indian's hand beneath it. The Anko calendar, kept by another Kiowa, records nothing of the treaty and remembers instead the killing of a Navajo (Diné) man. One Kiowa year-keeper made the treaty the winter's event; another did not.
entries.quote: The picture on the Set-t'an calendar is highly suggestive.
entries.source_note: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (BAE 17th Annual Report, 1898), Project Gutenberg #46479, fig. 142, p. 320

entries.headline: The commission's report names Sand Creek a massacre
entries.digest: The commission's report to President Johnson recounted how Black Kettle's people had been attacked at Sand Creek in November 1864 after being promised protection, and called the war that followed useless, costly and dishonourable. It found the Kiowa and Comanche had substantially kept their 1865 treaty and that most charges against them were without foundation. The report uses the period's language for Indigenous people, including 'savage'.
entries.quote: it was here, under the pledge of protection, that they were slaughtered
entries.source_note: Report to the President by the Indian Peace Commission, 7 Jan 1868 (Wikisource)

entries.headline: Signing a report that admits the 1865 terms failed
entries.digest: Henderson signed the commission's report with the others. It conceded that the Senate's amendment to the 1865 Little Arkansas treaty, requiring a reservation outside Kansas, had left the Cheyenne and Arapaho without any home but a hunting privilege, and recalled that the 1851 Fort Laramie treaty had kept their right to hunt and pass over their lands.
entries.source_note: Report to the President by the Indian Peace Commission, 7 Jan 1868 (Wikisource)

entries.headline: The Kiowa hold their Sun Dance at Medicine Lodge
entries.digest: The next summer the Kiowa held their Sun Dance on Medicine Lodge Creek, the treaty ground, and the calendars remember the season for a disastrous expedition against the Ute in which the taíme, a sacred image, was captured. The Kiowa were still using the country north of their new reservation as they always had.
entries.source_note: Mooney, Calendar History of the Kiowa Indians (BAE 17th Annual Report, 1898), Project Gutenberg #46479, fig. 143, p. 322 (index: 'Sun dance on Medicine-lodge creek')

entries.headline: Little Raven speaks in New York
entries.digest: Little Raven toured Washington and eastern cities in 1871 and spoke at Cooper Union in New York, carrying the Arapaho case to eastern audiences. In the Red River War of 1874–75 he kept his people neutral.
entries.source_note: Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture, 'Little Raven'

entries.place: Washington, DC, then near Fort Sill
entries.headline: A second journey to Washington, and death
entries.digest: Ten Bears went to Washington a second time in 1872 and attended a reception given by President Grant, agreeing before he left to an order bringing the Comanche within ten miles of Fort Sill. He died soon after his return, aged about eighty, on the reservation the treaty had made.
entries.source_note: EBSCO Research Starters 'Ten Bears'

entries.headline: Satanta, a prisoner, bargains for his release
entries.digest: Six years after Medicine Lodge, Satanta spoke at negotiations over his and Big Tree's release from the Texas penitentiary, where they had been held since the 1871 wagon-train raid. As interpreted and recorded for the Texas authorities, he argued that freeing him was the surest way to keep his people at peace.
entries.quote: The best thing to do for my people is to release me.
entries.source_note: Texas Indian Papers vol. 4, #224, Texas State Library and Archives Commission (speech as interpreted)

entries.headline: Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock: Congress may override Article 12
entries.digest: Writing for the Court, White rejected the Kiowa plaintiffs' claim that allotting their reservation without the consent of three-fourths of the adult men, as Article 12 of the Medicine Lodge treaty required, was unlawful. He held that Congress had plenary authority over tribal relations, a political power not reviewable by the courts, and could abrogate treaty provisions. The treaty's consent clause thereby lost its force against Congress.
entries.quote: Plenary authority over the tribal relations of the Indians
entries.source_note: Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock, 187 U.S. 553 (1903); Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture, 'Medicine Lodge Treaty'

entries.headline: Bent's recollection appears in print
entries.digest: Bent's memories of the council were printed in The Frontier as part of 'Forty Years with the Cheyennes', and were reprinted in Kansas in 1927 for the council's sixtieth anniversary. They are a late account by the one Cheyenne-born man on the treaty's witness list.
entries.source_note: Barber County Index, 29 Sept 1927, citing The Frontier, Feb. 1909, p. 5

entries.headline: The last survivor writes it down
entries.digest: Fifty-seven years later, the former governor wrote his memories of the council for the Chronicles of Oklahoma, describing himself as the only one of the party left to tell the tale. He closed with reflections on farming and the cost of living, a reminder of how far from the arbour the account was written.
entries.quote: the only one left to 'tell the tale'
entries.source_note: A. A. Taylor, 'Medicine Lodge Peace Council', Chronicles of Oklahoma 2:2 (June 1924), pp. 98-117 (Oklahoma Historical Society Gateway PDF), p. 117

claims.claim: Congress authorises a commission to remove the causes of war, secure the frontier and the railroads, and propose reservations
claims.evidence: Act of 20 July 1867 (15 Stat. 17); NPS summary

claims.claim: Satanta objects to soldiers killing buffalo for sport: his people kill only to live
The commission says it has made peace with the Oglala and Sicangu, and agrees to wait eight days for the Cheyenne
Offer: a reservation, houses, schools, farming tools and annuities, in return for the northern lands and peace with the railroads
The land south of the Arkansas belongs to the Kiowa and Comanche; he will not part with it or the buffalo, and wants no houses
The Comanche want to live on the open prairie, not in houses; the soldiers began the fighting
claims.evidence: Commission journal and press; 1927 reprint consulted

claims.claim: Kiowa, Comanche and Plains Apache reservation set between the 98th meridian, the Red River and its North Fork, and the Washita
Clothing each 15 October and $25,000 a year for thirty years; schools for at least twenty years; temporary hunting south of the Arkansas
claims.evidence: Treaty of 21 Oct 1867, Art. 10 and related articles (Mooney 1898)

claims.claim: No cession of the reservation valid without the signatures of three-fourths of the adult men
The country between the Arkansas and the South Platte is Cheyenne country
claims.evidence: Press reports as summarised by Jones (1966) and NPS

claims.claim: Spoken promise: the Cheyenne may hunt north of the Arkansas while living south of it — not written into the treaty
claims.evidence: Correspondents' reports via Jones (1966) and NPS

claims.claim: A reporter asks for the hunting promise to be written in; Henderson refuses
claims.evidence: Missouri Republican correspondent, via Jones (1966) and NPS

claims.claim: Cheyenne and Arapaho reservation between the Kansas line, the Arkansas and the Cimarron; hunting only south of the Arkansas while buffalo last
claims.evidence: Treaty of 28 Oct 1867, Arts. 2 and 11, 15 Stat. 593

claims.claim: Sand Creek was a massacre of people under a pledge of protection; the war that followed was useless and dishonourable
claims.evidence: Report of the Indian Peace Commission, 7 Jan 1868

claims.claim: The Senate ratifies the Medicine Lodge treaties; proclaimed 19 Aug (Cheyenne–Arapaho) and 25 Aug 1868 (Kiowa–Comanche–Apache)
claims.evidence: Kappler; Mooney 1898; OSU Tribal Treaties Database

claims.claim: Congress has plenary power over tribal relations and may abrogate treaty terms, including Article 12's consent rule

convergences.label: Satanta and Little Raven ride out to meet the column
convergences.note: The correspondent sees a picturesque arrival and a buffalo hunt; Little Raven and Satanta come to look over the commission before it reaches their camps, and the next day Satanta turns the reporters' buffalo shooting into his first argument.

convergences.label: The preliminary council and the eight-day wait
convergences.note: Taylor opens with news of peace in the north; the Tribune's man reports the delay as a setback, while for the Cheyenne the wait was time to finish their own business on the Cimarron before coming in.

convergences.label: The grand council opens
convergences.note: The president's opening, the secretary's journal and Black Kettle's near-silence: the official record begins with the Cheyenne almost absent from it.

convergences.label: The great speeches: Henderson, Satanta, Ten Bears
convergences.note: Henderson offers houses and schools; Satanta and Ten Bears refuse houses and claim the land and the open prairie; Little Raven asks for what was owed. Stanley writes it all down in the interpreters' English that is all that survives.

convergences.label: The Kiowa, Comanche and Plains Apache sign
convergences.note: The men who had refused houses the day before put their marks to a paper promising houses, schools and a reservation, with a last-minute hunting concession; what each side thought had been agreed is not the same.

convergences.label: The Cheyenne arrive in five columns
convergences.note: Black Kettle's long effort ends in a mounted charge that the reporters found thrilling and alarming; Taylor's later memory turns it into a story of being fooled.

convergences.label: The Cheyenne and Arapaho council and signing
convergences.note: Henderson demands the northern country; Buffalo Chief claims it; Henderson promises hunting aloud; Fayel asks for it in writing and is refused; Bent interprets the signing; the secretary and the correspondent witness it. The written Article 11 and the spoken promise part company here.

convergences.label: Timber-hill winter and the commission's report
convergences.note: The Kiowa year-keeper remembers a handshake under a wooded hill; the commission in Washington writes a long indictment of Sand Creek and a plan for reservations. Two records of the same season, one a picture, one a state paper.

ties.note: Father and son: the commission's president brought his 19-year-old son as an assistant secretary.
Taylor called Stanley his friend and travelled with him on the commission's journeys; both signed the Cheyenne treaty as witnesses.
The reporter asked the senator to write the hunting promise into the treaty, and was refused.
On 28 October Henderson demanded the land between the Arkansas and the Platte, and Buffalo Chief claimed it for the Cheyenne.
Leaders of allied nations, Kiowa and Comanche, who spoke against houses at the same council and signed the same treaty on 21 October.
Stanley's dispatches are a main source for Satanta's speeches, and a 1978 article on Stanley's Medicine Lodge reporting is built around him.
Bent was in Black Kettle's camp when it was attacked at Sand Creek in 1864, and interpreted at the treaty Black Kettle signed in 1867.
Both appear on the witness list of the Cheyenne and Arapaho treaty, the interpreter and the secretary.
Arapaho and Cheyenne peace chiefs whose people shared the 1861, 1865 and 1867 treaties and the reservation of 1867.
Taylor praised Little Raven's speech on damages and Sand Creek above all others he heard.
Set-t'an's calendar is a year-count of Satanta's own nation; its Medicine Lodge winter records the treaty Satanta signed.
The Court in 1903 construed Article 12 of the treaty Ten Bears signed for the Comanche, and held Congress could set it aside.
White served as secretary to the commission Taylor presided over and kept its journal.

threads_out.note: The commission's 1868 report quotes the 1851 Fort Laramie treaty's preservation of the right to hunt and pass over the lands between the Arkansas and the Platte, the same country Henderson asked the Cheyenne to give up at Medicine Lodge. After Medicine Lodge the commission went north to make the Fort Laramie treaty of 1868.

Henry M. Stanley, the young correspondent who signed the Cheyenne treaty as a witness, was hired by the New York Herald soon after and in 1871 found David Livingstone at Ujiji; his Medicine Lodge reports helped launch that career.

The commission's soldiers, Sherman, Terry and Augur, were Union generals of the Civil War, and Henderson co-wrote the Thirteenth Amendment; the postwar push of railroads and settlers west is the background the 1867 act names.

Article 11 tied the southern nations' hunting rights to the buffalo lasting 'in such numbers as to justify the chase'; by the late 1870s the southern herds were gone, and Treaty 6 in Canada (1876) was negotiated against the same collapse, with its famine clause.
